Females of the Checkered wolf eel reach a maximum total length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], a modest size that aligns with the life-history strategies of deep-dwelling zoarcids. This ultimate length is attained only after several years of sustained somatic investment in the cold, prey-sparse environments typical of this species. At the opposite end of the size spectrum, the wet weight at birth is remarkably low at 0.0477 grams [Wwb = 0.0477 grams], a direct consequence of the small egg diameter of 4.5 millimeters that characterizes the yolky, demersal eggs of the genus. These minute neonates are fully dependent on endogenous reserves during a prolonged yolk-sac larval phase, a risky early-life strategy that demands a high rate of maternal investment to offset the elevated mortality typical of small-bodied teleost larvae.

Experimental rearing under controlled thermal conditions has clarified several key life-history milestones for this species. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C], a value close to the in situ bottom temperatures of its bathyal habitat, the age at birth or time from oviposition to larval emergence is approximately 150 days [ab = approximately 150 days]. Such an extended incubation period is not unusual among Arctic and subarctic fishes and likely reflects the decelerated metabolic and developmental rates imposed by the cold thermal regime. From the moment of chorion rupture, the newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are immediately exposed to the selective pressures of a patchy food environment, and their small size means that rapid progress through the yolk absorption stage is crucial for survival to the onset of exogenous feeding.

The transition to sexual maturation represents a major life-history bottleneck for Checkered wolf eel. Under the same thermal conditions of 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at roughly 2 years [tp = roughly 2 years], a comparatively slow developmental pace that underscores the species' affiliation with a slow, high-survival life-history strategy. At this pubertal stage, females measure 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters] in total length and have a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 4.9 grams [Wwp = 4.9 grams]. This body mass at the onset of gonadal activity is substantially less than the projected ultimate mass, indicating that a considerable portion of female somatic growth continues well after reproductive capability is first attained, consistent with the pattern observed in many deep-water benthic fishes.

Reproductive output in this species, while low compared to many epipelagic teleosts, is closely tuned to the cold thermal environment it inhabits. At the habitual temperature of 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C], the maximum reproductive rate translates to approximately 0.088 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.088 eggs per day], a modest daily output that likely reflects constraints on both female body cavity volume and the energetic costs of vitellogenesis in near-freezing waters. The cost of this effort is partially offset by the ultimate wet weight of 17.2 grams [Wwi = 17.2 grams] attained by full-grown females, a body size that provides a greater capacity for yolk production and batch fecundity relative to smaller conspecifics. The relationship between length and mass, derived from a length-weight conversion, suggests a strongly positive allometric relationship in this species.

Finally, the Checkered wolf eel exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] when maintained at 1.8 °C [T = 1.8 °C], a figure that places it among the longer-lived members of the Lycenchelys genus. This extended longevity is a classic correlate of the slow life-history strategy observed in many high-latitude and deep-sea fishes, where delayed reproduction and low metabolic rates are traded against a greater probability of surviving to an advanced age. The ultimate wet weight of 17.2 grams [Wwi = 17.2 grams] is the terminal limit of somatic growth reached by females before the onset of senescence and natural death. Together, these demographic parameters paint a portrait of a species finely adapted to a cold, stable, and resource-limited environment, where each reproductive event is maximized relative to the slow pace of somatic and gonadal development.
